analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal land to oil, gas, coal, and mining while weakening environmental review and pollution fees.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-204 in March 2023, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the government to hold frequent oil and gas lease sales on federal land, cut the royalty rates energy companies pay to drill there, and speed up permits by narrowing environmental review, limiting court challenges, and letting states' water-quality objections be bypassed for gas pipelines. It also repeals fees on methane pollution, eliminates federal programs that paid for home energy upgrades in low-income households, and restricts sales of emergency oil reserves to China and other sanctioned countries. Supporters argued it would lower energy prices; most of its direct financial benefits go to energy and mining companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, coal and hardrock mining companies, LNG exporters, and petroleum refiners gain the most: mandated lease sales, lower royalties, repeal of a methane emissions fee, faster permits, weakened environmental review, and exemptions from certain air and hazard rules. Households that use gas stoves keep access guaranteed by statute, and emergency reserve oil can no longer be sold to China or sanctioned countries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold quarterly onshore oil and gas lease sales, at least four per year in each eligible state, and to replace any canceled or under-bid sale [S3].

Cuts federal royalties and fees for energy development by repealing the rate increases enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, and states that onshore royalties should be no more than 12.5% [S3].

Requires Interior to issue permits for all completed pending drilling applications within 30 days and speeds environmental reviews across energy, mining, and transmission projects, with agencies owing applicants $100 per day for missed deadlines [S3].

Removes the 'public interest' test for natural gas imports and exports, making FERC the sole reviewer of gas pipeline environmental impacts, and limits states' Clean Water Act veto over interstate pipelines [S3].
Bars the President from declaring a fracking moratorium without an act of Congress, and bars the Energy Department from enforcing any rule limiting access to gas kitchen ranges and ovens [S3].
Prohibits selling or exporting oil drawn from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to China, North Korea, Russia, Iran, or sanctioned entities [S3].
Bans entities owned or controlled by China or the Communist Party of China from acquiring interests in federal energy lands, farmland, renewable energy lands, or mining claims [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers lose royalty revenue from the lower rates; communities near drilling, mining, and pipelines face weaker environmental review, limited ability to sue, and looser air and hazardous-waste rules; low-income households lose the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund and the home energy rebate and contractor-training programs the bill repeals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-income households, nearby communities, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Repeals the Clean Air Act's methane emissions charge and its incentive program for oil and gas systems, removing a fee on the industry's largest source of greenhouse gas pollution [S3].
Eliminates the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, which funded emissions-reducing projects in low-income and disadvantaged communities, and rescinds unspent money [S3].
Repeals the high-efficiency electric home rebate program, home energy contractor training grants, and building energy code assistance, rescinding unspent funds [S3].

Narrows environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act: agencies must consider only effects with a close causal relationship, alternatives must be economically feasible, documents face page limits, lawsuits must be filed within 120 days, and courts cannot halt projects unless they find imminent, substantial environmental harm with no other remedy [S3].
Exempts refineries using hydrofluoric acid alkylation units from assessing safer technologies, even though an accidental release of the acid can form a toxic vapor cloud [S3].
Replaces the Clean Water Act Section 401 process with a FERC-led review for interstate gas pipelines, so a state can no longer deny a certification on its own water-quality grounds [S3].
Reduces the share of offshore energy revenue going to the Treasury and the Land and Water Conservation Fund by shifting more to Gulf producing states [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Permitting delays are a real cost, and parts of this bill — faster transmission-line reviews, geothermal permitting, categories exempted from review — would help projects of all kinds, including renewable ones. But the core of the bill cuts what energy companies pay the public (royalties, methane fees), mandates more leasing, and makes pollution-related challenges harder to bring, while the claimed benefit to household energy bills is indirect and uncertain. At the same time it repeals programs that directly cut energy costs for low-income homeowners. On balance, the bill's direct and certain benefits flow to energy and mining companies, and its direct and certain costs fall on taxpayers, nearby communities, and low-income households.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line 225-204 vote in March 2023, but the Senate never scheduled a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The House passed H.R. 1 on March 30, 2023, by a vote of 225 to 204; 221 of 222 Republicans voted yes, as did 4 Democrats, while 203 Democrats voted no [S8].
All 207 Democrats present voted for a motion to recommit the bill to committee, a last procedural attempt to change or stop it, which failed 207-222 [S7].
After House passage, the Senate took no recorded action on the bill, and it received no vote there before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in the Senate, oil, gas, coal, and mining companies did not get the mandated lease sales, royalty cuts, or repeal of the methane fee. Low-income households kept the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund and home energy rebate programs through the end of the Congress, and the Treasury kept the higher royalty rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Homeowners and the Treasury, not energy companies

for.name: Steve Scalise
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 1 as the House Republican majority's first bill and led it to passage.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 1 to the Senate floor for a vote after House passage.

against.name: President Biden
against.what_they_did: The administration publicly opposed the bill and threatened a veto, calling it a giveaway to oil companies.

against.name: Katie Porter
against.what_they_did: Offered the motion to recommit the bill, which failed 207-222 with all Democrats in favor and all Republicans opposed.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was nearly unanimous among Republicans (221 of 222) with just 4 of 213 voting Democrats in support; the failed motion to recommit split perfectly on party lines, 207-222 [S7][S8].

industries.note: The bill mandates quarterly lease sales on federal land, cuts the royalties and fees producers pay, repeals the methane emissions charge, and speeds permits while limiting environmental review and lawsuits. The savings flow to producers; the public loses revenue and pollution safeguards.
Requires approval of pending federal coal lease applications, restarts canceled lease sales, and nullifies the 2016 order that paused federal coal leasing for a program-wide environmental review.

Extends fast-track permitting from critical minerals to all minerals, allows exploration with up to five acres of surface disturbance on notice, permits mine support activities before a deposit is confirmed, and bars most mining land withdrawals without extensive assessments.

industries.industry: LNG exporters and gas pipeline companies
industries.note: Deems gas exports in the public interest, makes FERC the sole environmental reviewer for interstate pipelines, and replaces state water-quality certification, removing the main levers states and opponents used to block or condition projects.

Exempts refineries with hydrofluoric acid alkylation units from assessing safer technologies and grants critical-energy facilities interim hazardous waste permits, flexible air permits, and emergency Clean Air Act waivers.

The streamlined environmental review, categorical exclusions, and longer rights-of-way apply to transmission lines, geothermal, and storage as well as fossil projects, but new GAO studies are required before offshore wind lease sales in several planning areas.

industries.industry: Home energy efficiency and electrification contractors
industries.note: The bill repeals the home rebate program and contractor training grants those businesses were built to deliver, removing a federal revenue stream along with the household savings.
